title: Integral realization of root data and central lattice isogenies
statement:
An integral group scheme means a group object over $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, using the group diagrams of [def-sc-group-scheme] over this base [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. A reductive integral group scheme is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], affine [pqf-def-affine-morphism], finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation], with connected geometric fibres [def-weil-connected-scheme] and no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup in any geometric fibre. Unipotent means that in a faithful matrix representation all geometric points are unipotent matrices, so $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$. A split maximal torus is a closed subgroup [def-weil-closed-immersion] $U\simeq D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ with fibrewise maximal tori, for a finite-rank free abelian group $M$; $D_A(M)=\operatorname{Spec}A[M]$ has the Hopf operations of [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. Characters and cocharacters are homomorphisms to and from $\mathbf G_m$, paired by $\chi\circ\lambda(t)=t^{\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle}$. A reduced root datum $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ consists of a finite-rank free abelian group $M$, its integer dual $M^\vee$, finite subsets $\Phi\subset M\setminus\{0\}$ and $\Phi^\vee\subset M^\vee\setminus\{0\}$ in bijection $\alpha\mapsto\alpha^\vee$, with $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. The reflections $s_\alpha(m)=m-\langle m,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and their duals permute the roots and coroots compatibly, the group generated by the reflections is finite, and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. Every reduced root datum is the root datum of a reductive integral group scheme $G$ with a specified split maximal torus $U=D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$; the group root datum and its geometric-fibre interpretation are those of [lem-sfb-integral-split-root-datum]. Let $(G_i,U_i)$, $i=0,1$, be two such split integral groups, with root data $(M_i,\Phi_i,M_i^\vee,\Phi_i^\vee)$. Suppose $u:M_0\hookrightarrow M_1$ has finite cokernel and there is a bijection $b:\Phi_1\to\Phi_0$ such that
$$u(b(\alpha))=\alpha,\qquad u^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=b(\alpha)^\vee\quad(\alpha\in\Phi_1),$$
where $u^\vee$ is restriction of integer-valued functionals. There exists a homomorphism $f:G_1\to G_0$ restricting to $D_{\mathbf Z}(u):U_1\to U_0$. It is finite, faithfully flat and finitely presented, and its scheme-theoretic kernel is the closed central subgroup $D_{\mathbf Z}(M_1/u(M_0))\subseteq U_1$. Finite means affine with finite coordinate module over the target, faithfully flat means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] and surjective, and central means commuting with every point after every algebra extension. The same statements and the indicated torus restriction and kernel description hold after every ring base change $\mathbf Z\to A$, including to nonreduced rings. No invertibility assumption on the order of $M_1/u(M_0)$ is made; in particular its diagonalizable kernel need not be smooth. Empty root systems and rank zero are allowed.

source.place: Theorem 6.1.16(1),(2), printed p.196; Definition 6.1.8 and Example 6.1.9, p.191 (all root exponents equal one); Definition 3.3.9 and Proposition 3.3.10, p.103; Corollary 3.3.6(1), p.101, and Appendix B.1 for the kernel inside the maximal torus. Read online; WANTED locally as literature/conrad-reductive-group-schemes.pdf. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group structural theorem.

proof.text: First put a base on the prescribed abstract root datum. The lattice-embedding lemma restricts the rationalized pairing to the root span $V$ and its dual, giving a spanning reduced crystallographic root pairing. Apply the rational base-existence lemma there. Its independent simple roots, with the same integer expansions of all roots, give a base $\Delta\subset\Phi$ in $M$; the complementary central directions impose no additional condition. For $A=\mathbf Z$, pinned split classification now gives a pinned split realization of this based datum. Forget the base and generators. Its specified torus is $D_{\mathbf Z}(M)$ and its geometric root data are the prescribed ones, which proves the existence assertion. For $\Phi=\varnothing$ use the empty base, so this also includes tori and rank zero.

source.place: Theorems 6.1.16(2), 6.1.17, printed pp.196-197; base choice as in Definition 6.1.1, p.186. Rational base choice is the cited root-pairing lemma.

proof.text: We will also apply the isomorphism clause to given integral groups with a specified split maximal torus. Here are the pinning hypotheses explicitly. Integral split root data give constant roots and free rank-one root modules. The relative tangent-weight theorem gives a finite projective tangent module, its weight decomposition and arbitrary base-change compatibility. Its zero-weight part is the tangent module of the torus centralizer, by the relative centralizer theorem. On each geometric fibre the self-centralizer theorem identifies this centralizer with the maximal torus. Thus $\operatorname{Lie}(U)\to\mathfrak g_0$ is an isomorphism: both are finite free over $\mathbf Z$ (a finite projective module embeds in a finite free module, so apply the subgroup-freeness lemma), and its matrix is invertible modulo every prime and over $\mathbf Q$; its determinant is consequently $\pm1$. We obtain exactly $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(U)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$. Choose generators for the simple-root lines. Together with any chosen base this satisfies the pinned-realization definition, without a field hypothesis on the integral group.

source.place: Definition 5.1.1, Example 5.1.4, Definition 6.1.1 and proof of Corollary 6.2.11(2), printed pp.136-137,186,210; explicit tangent verification using the cited relative statements.

proof.text: Set $L=u(M_0)\subseteq M_1$ and $C=M_1/L$. Character duality gives the closed inclusion $K=D_{\mathbf Z}(C)\hookrightarrow U_1$, the kernel of $D_{\mathbf Z}(u)$, and the quotient $U_1/K=D_{\mathbf Z}(L)$. Every $\alpha\in\Phi_1$ equals $u(b(\alpha))$, hence lies in $L$ and has trivial restriction to $K$. The relative centre-weight-kernel theorem identifies $Z(G_1)$ inside $U_1$ with the intersection of these character kernels. Therefore $K\subseteq Z(G_1)$ as subgroup schemes, including on nonreduced test rings. Since $C$ is finite, $\mathbf Z[C]$ has the finite basis $(e_c)_{c\in C}$, so $K$ is finite over $\mathbf Z$. This uses no inversion of $|C|$.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.6(1), Appendix B.1, and the central quotient argument of Lemma 6.3.1, printed pp.101,212-213,280-281.

proof.text: Apply the relative central multiplicative quotient theorem over the nonzero Noetherian ring $\mathbf Z$ to $G_1$ and $K$. It supplies a reductive integral group $H=G_1/K$, a faithfully flat finitely presented homomorphism $q:G_1\to H$ with kernel $K$, and its torsor identity $G_1\times K\simeq G_1\times_HG_1$. The same theorem makes $V=U_1/K$ a maximal torus of $H$, with inverse image $U_1$. Character duality identifies $V=D_{\mathbf Z}(L)$; the isomorphism $M_0\xrightarrow{u}L$ identifies $V$ with $U_0$. The quotient torus map then pulls a character $m\in M_0$ back to $u(m)$, as required.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.5 and Lemma 6.3.1, printed pp.100-101,212-213; Appendix B.1 for the torus quotient.

proof.text: The map $q$ is finite as well. It is an fppf covering, and hence an fpqc covering by the fppf-to-fpqc lemma. Pulling $q$ back along itself gives $G_1\times K\to G_1$ by the torsor identity. Since $G_1$ is affine and $\mathbf Z[C]$ is free on the finite set $C$, this projection has coordinate algebra $\mathcal O(G_1)[C]$, finite free over $\mathcal O(G_1)$, and is finite. Apply fpqc descent of finite morphisms to this covering of $H$. This proves finiteness of $q$, including when a prime divides $|C|$.

source.place: Definition 3.3.9 and Proposition 3.3.10, printed p.103; here finiteness is verified by the torsor identity and Stacks 02LA (descent.tex, lemma-descending-property-finite).

proof.text: Compute the root datum of $(H,V)$, rather than identifying it merely from dimensions. The integral split-root theorem supplies its constant datum. Choose a base and pinning of $(H,V)$ as in steps 1-2; the positive-root Borel theorem supplies a Borel containing $V$. On every geometric fibre of $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf Z$, the central-isogeny Borel-root compatibility theorem applies to $q$: its target is reductive, its source is smooth connected affine of finite type, and its kernel is the finite central $K_k$. It identifies roots by pullback $L\hookrightarrow M_1$ and carries each source coroot to its restriction to $L$. Consequently the roots of $H$ are exactly $\Phi_1\subset L$, and the coroot of $\alpha$ is $\alpha^\vee|_L$. Under $u:M_0\simeq L$ these are $b(\alpha)$ and $u^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=b(\alpha)^\vee$. Thus the specified torus identification extends to an isomorphism of the integral root datum of $(H,V)$ with that of $(G_0,U_0)$. The integral datum is determined by these lattice subsets and functionals, so geometric-fibre compatibility is being used for root data, not as a claim that arbitrary group maps are determined by their geometric fibres.

source.place: Lemma 6.3.1, printed pp.212-213; root and coroot compatibility under central isogenies, Definition 6.1.8, Example 6.1.9 and Proposition 6.1.13, pp.191-194.

proof.text: Choose a base in the datum of $G_0$ as in step 1 and its corresponding base in the identified datum of $H$. Equip the two groups with pinnings using the verified hypotheses of step 2. The isomorphism part of pinned split classification supplies an integral group isomorphism $h:H\xrightarrow{\sim}G_0$ inducing this particular lattice identification on the tori. Set $f=h\circ q$. Its torus restriction is $D_{\mathbf Z}(u)$, not just an unspecified torus isogeny. Composition with an isomorphism preserves the finite coordinate-module property, faithful flatness and finite presentation, so $f$ has all three. Since $h$ has trivial kernel, $\ker(f)=\ker(q)=K$, with exactly the inclusion $D_{\mathbf Z}(C)\subseteq U_1\subseteq G_1$ constructed above.

source.place: Theorem 6.1.17, printed p.197, applied to the explicitly identified quotient datum; compare the central quotient construction of Lemma 6.3.1.

proof.text: Finally let $\mathbf Z\to A$ be any unital ring map. The fppf covering $q$ stays an fppf covering after base change, so it stays flat and surjective; finite presentation is also preserved by arbitrary base change. Finiteness can be checked directly: tensor a finite list of coordinate-module generators with $A$; it still generates the base-changed coordinate algebra over the base-changed target. The quotient theorem and character duality identify the pulled-back quotient and kernel with $H_A$ and $D_A(C)$, and the Hopf formula $e_m\mapsto e_{u(m)}$ shows that the torus restriction remains $D_A(u)$. The base change $h_A$ is an isomorphism with inverse $(h^{-1})_A$, giving all assertions for $f_A$. Centrality persists because any $A$-algebra extension is also a $\mathbf Z$-algebra extension in the defining commutation condition. No flatness or reducedness of $A$ has entered. For the zero ring the schemes are empty and the same coordinate formulas give every assertion; the nonzero-base structural theorems were used only over $\mathbf Z$.

source.place: Appendix B.1 and Corollary 3.3.5; Stacks 021O (topologies.tex, lemma-fppf) and 01TS for base change of finite presentation.
